charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Keppel DC REIT: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

dpu.title: Distribution per Unit (DPU)
dpu.content:
DPU is the cash distribution paid per unit for the period, in Singapore cents equivalent (reported here in S$).

For Keppel DC REIT: DPU is the per-unit compounding rate that matters, not aggregate distributable income — the DCF uses the 5yr DPU CAGR (2.5%) as the base-case growth proxy because aggregate growth has been diluted by unit issuance (the Oct-2025 preferential offering added 10.5% more units).

What to watch:

  • DPU growth versus aggregate distributable-income growth (the gap is dilution)
  • Half-year DPU swings from acquisition timing or FX hedge rolls

distributableIncome.title: Distributable income and net property income
distributableIncome.content:
Distributable income is the cash REIT managers actually distribute to unitholders — net property income less finance costs, management fees and tax, adjusted for non-cash items. Net property income is rental income less property operating expenses, before financing.

For Keppel DC REIT: this stands in for AFFO, which isn't a line Singapore REITs disclose under that name; distributable income already nets out financing costs, so it's the cleanest owner-cash figure available.

What to watch:

  • Distributable income growing slower than net property income (rising finance costs as hedges roll off)
  • The spread between the two as a rough proxy for interest and fee drag

navGearing.title: NAV per unit and aggregate leverage (gearing)
navGearing.content:
NAV per unit is net asset value divided by units in issue — the REIT's book value per unit, revalued periodically under IAS 40. Gearing is total borrowings as a percentage of total deposited property value, the REIT-specific leverage ratio regulators cap (MAS limit is 50%).

For Keppel DC REIT: NAV/unit (S$1.73 at H1 FY2026) is the DCF's asset-value cross-check against the capitalised-AFFO intrinsic value; gearing of 34% (71% hedged) is comfortably under the regulatory cap but each +100bp of rate resets cuts interest cover materially.

What to watch:

  • Gearing drifting up from debt-funded acquisitions
  • NAV/unit growth outpacing or lagging DPU growth

occupancyWale.title: Occupancy and WALE
occupancyWale.content:
Occupancy is leased floor area as a percentage of total available; WALE (weighted average lease expiry) is the lease-weighted average years to expiry across the portfolio.

For Keppel DC REIT: only FY2021 has these disclosed in the filings extracted so far (98.3% occupancy, 7.5yr WALE) — later annual reports summarise occupancy qualitatively or by data-hall rather than a single portfolio figure. A single historical point is shown for context, not a trend.

What to watch:

  • Single-hyperscaler concentration (43.5% of 1H2026 rental income per the DCF) makes WALE and occupancy more fragile than the headline numbers suggest
  • Renewal timing clustering in any one year

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Keppel DC REIT: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Keppel DC REIT: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Keppel DC REIT: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Keppel DC REIT: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Keppel DC REIT: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Keppel DC REIT: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Keppel DC REIT: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality
